name: Cycle to Time Converter
blurb: instruction cycles to microseconds and back at a clock
intro: Time = cycles × clocks per cycle / clock frequency, and back. It also gives the busy-wait loop count for that time and the prescaler and reload a 8-, 16- or 32-bit timer needs to count it, with the rounding error.

inputs.label: Clocks per instruction cycle
inputs.help: 1 for AVR, ARM Cortex-M, RISC-V; 4 for PIC10/12/16/18 (Fosc/4); 12 for a classic 8051.

inputs.label: Cycles per delay-loop pass
inputs.help: Instruction cycles one pass of your busy-wait loop takes (e.g. 4 for AVR _delay_loop_2, 3 for a Cortex-M SUBS/BNE loop).

examples.title: How long are 1000 cycles on a 16 MHz AVR?
Cycles for 10 µs on a PIC18 at 64 MHz

usage: Choose c2t (give cycles) or t2c (give time in seconds), the clock in Hz, the clocks per instruction cycle and the instruction cycles per delay-loop pass. It returns the time or cycle count, the cycle period, the delay-loop count, a table of the same count at common clocks, and timer prescaler/reload settings (8-bit, 16-bit, 32-bit, any or power-of-two prescaler) with their actual time and error.
sources: t = N × CPC / fclk: definition; PIC instruction cycle = Fosc/4 (Microchip PIC16/PIC18 datasheets), 8051 machine cycle = 12 clocks (Intel MCS-51 manual)
Timer period = (PSC + 1)(ARR + 1) / f_timer: STM32 reference manuals (general-purpose timers); AVR prescalers 1/8/64/256/1024: ATmega328P datasheet, Timer/Counter1
